title: Longest Stretch Within a Spread
statement:
You get an array nums of sensor readings and a tolerance limit. A stretch is a contiguous, non-empty run of readings. It is steady if the largest reading in it minus the smallest reading in it is at most limit.

Return the length of the longest steady stretch.

examples.why: [9, 6, 7] has spread 3. Adding 5 on the left makes it 4, and adding 2 on the right makes it 7.
All values equal, so the spread is 0 everywhere.
Neighbours always differ by at least 4, so no two adjacent readings fit together. Checking only the first and last element of a stretch would accept [1, 6, 2] wrongly.

hints: If a stretch is steady, so is every shorter stretch inside it. What does that suggest about the left edge as the right edge moves?
A sliding window works: extend on the right, and shrink from the left while max − min is too large. The hard part is knowing the window's max and min quickly.
Keep two deques of indexes: one with decreasing values (front is the max) and one with increasing values (front is the min). Drop fronts that fall out of the window.

explain.intuition:
Shrinking a stretch can only lower its spread, so if [l..r] is steady then every stretch inside it is too. That means the best left edge never moves backwards as r grows, which is exactly the sliding window shape: add nums[r], then advance l until the window is steady again.

The window needs its current max and min after every change. A monotonic deque gives both in amortized O(1). The max deque keeps indexes whose values decrease from front to back: when a new value arrives, anything smaller behind it can never be the max again, so pop it. The front is the max. The min deque is the mirror image. When l passes the index at a front, drop it. This is the same structure as "peak of every window", only with a window whose size is decided by the data.
steps: Keep l = 0, a decreasing deque maxQ and an increasing deque minQ of indexes.
For each r: pop from the back of maxQ while its value is < nums[r], then push r. Do the mirror for minQ.
While nums[maxQ.front] − nums[minQ.front] > limit: move l right, and drop any front index that is now < l.
Record r − l + 1 and return the largest value seen.
pitfalls: Comparing only the window's first and last element. The extremes can sit anywhere inside, as in the third example.
Using JavaScript's Array.prototype.shift for the deque fronts. It is O(n), which turns the window into O(n²) on large inputs. Keep a head index instead.
Shrinking by only one step per r while still recording the window size. Either shrink fully, or know why the one-step version only works for the maximum length.

solutions.title: Every start, extend while steady
solutions.idea: For each start, extend to the right tracking the running max and min, and stop when the spread exceeds the limit.

solutions.title: Sliding window with two monotonic deques
solutions.idea: A decreasing deque tracks the window max and an increasing one tracks the min. Shrink from the left while max − min exceeds the limit.

followups: Solve it with a sorted multiset (or two heaps with lazy deletion) instead of deques. What does it cost?
Return the start index of the longest steady stretch, choosing the leftmost one on ties.
